newsitem.title: USA: Alaskan salmon season opens with huge catch.
newsitem.headline: Alaskan salmon season opens with huge catch.

text.p: Alaska's commercial salmon season opened with Prince William Sound fishermen hauling in more than six times the anticipated number of Copper River sockeyes, state officials said on Tuesday.

Fishermen who ended the 24-hour opening last Friday netted 190,000 of the red salmon, easily breaking last year's first-day Copper River harvest record of 103,000, said Herman Savikko, spokesman for the Alaska Department of Fish and Game.
"This year, they just completely blew people out of the water," he said.

Last year's Copper River sockeye harvest totaled a record 2.4 million fish. That is at least twice the average in years before recent bumper harvests, Savikko said. "Prior to the astounding catches, they were doing quite well if they got a million to 1.2 million," he said.
The Copper River catch, which also includes some chinook salmon, runs from mid-May to late June and is the first summer commercial salmon harvest in Alaska.
It is conducted in spurts, with the Department of Fish and Game generally holding two 24-hour openings a week. A second 24-hour opening for this season was held on Monday and Tuesday.
The Copper River salmon, like all Alaska salmon, have benefited from favorable ocean conditions, Savikko said.
The large harvest is likely to depress prices for the Copper River salmon, prized for their stong taste and rich red color and mostly sold to domestic markets, Savikko said.
Last year, fishermen got $1.90 to $1.95 a pound at the start of the season, a price that dropped to $1.75 weeks later, he said.
This year, prices have started at $1.55 a pound, he said.
Statewide, Alaska's commercial fishermen are expected to net 171 million salmon this year, under the 217 million record set in 1995 but still a large harvest, Savikko said.
But fishermen may ignore much of the returning fish, especially low-value pink salmon, if prices are too low, he said.
"I think overall we're going to have a large number of fish returning, and it's up to the markets as to how much of that is caught," he said.

Meanwhile, Gov. Tony Knowles criticized Canadian officials for what he called the untimely interruption of negotiations between fishermen over problems relating to the U.S.-Canada Pacific Salmon Treaty.

The Democratic governor blamed Canadian politics, including the national elections set for June 2, for the government's decision to break off talks between fishermen from Alaska, British Columbia and the Pacific Northwest states.
Those "stakeholder" negotiations, Knowles said, came close to producing solutions to disputes over harvests of chinook salmon, which migrate through Alaskan, Canadian and Pacific Northwest waters.
"They did more in three months than the governments did in 12 years," Knowles said on a call-in program broadcast on Tuesday over public radio.
Knowles said he had sent letters to U.S. Secretary of State Madeleine Albright and Canadian Ambassador Raymond Chretien protesting the end of the fishermen's negotiations.
Government negotiations over Pacific Salmon Treaty issues were under way on Tuesday in Seattle.
The alternative stakeholder talks were set up by Knowles and the Democratic governors of Washington and Oregon.
